#1214. 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

In the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

#1212. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Brighton reached the Conference League after brushing Tromso aside in the play-offs with a 4-0 aggregate victory and enter the competition as one of the favourites.

Fabian Hurzeler’s side have made an excellent start to the Premier League season, sitting third with 18 goals scored in six matches, and will hope to replicate their domestic form in this European encounter against Lithuanian minnows Kauno Zalgiris.

English clubs have won the Conference League in three of the five seasons since the competition’s creation, with Brighton’s bitter rivals Crystal Palace previously lifting the trophy in May.

Hurzeler has made eight changes to the team which beat Sunderland last Saturday, with Jack Hinshelwood notably returning to the line-up.

Whatever the result, this is a momentous night for Bournemouth, who are poised for their first European fixture at home in the club’s history as they welcome Austrian outfit Sturm Graz to the Vitality Stadium.

Bournemouth kickstarted their inaugural Europa League campaign with an unforgettable 2-1 victory over Real Sociedad on September 17 in San Sebastian, thanks to first-half goals from Justin Kluivert and Rayan.

This was just Bournemouth’s second win of the season in all competitions, with the club having made a slow start to the campaign under new head coach Marco Rose. That other triumph arrived in the EFL Cup, when Bournemouth thrashed Lincoln City 4-0 at the start of September.

The buzz around Bournemouth’s European exploits have partially masked a very poor opening to the Premier League season as Rose’s winless side languish in 18th, with only three points from six games. They suffered a heavy 5-1 loss to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge in their previous outing.

#1211. Man United are in the relegation zone on merit and will need all of Mauricio Pochettino's coaching powers to get them out of it - they are chronically short of form and have forgotten how to win, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Published: 02:00 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 10:28 EST, 24 November 2026

As the fourth goal flew in and Anfield rejoiced once again, Mauricio Pochettino stood on the touchline with his arms folded and turned to the Manchester United bench with an air of resignation.

What can he do to improve this shambles of a team? What could anyone do? United could change their head coach every game, but without the tools to do the job, the result will be largely the same.

Chief executive Omar Berrada said in an interview during the week that United have improved since the summer, but who is he trying to kid? They are in the relegation zone on merit, and it will need all of Pochettino's coaching powers to get them out of it.

He emerged from the tunnel shortly before 4.30pm here dressed smartly in blue, and after greeting Andoni Iraola and his staff, spent a few moments gathering his thoughts while You'll Never Walk Alone echoed around Anfield.

The game plan was in tatters inside 13 minutes, though, as he watched United go two goals and one man down. There was much finger wagging from Pochettino when Leny Yoro was somewhat harshly sent off, but the decision was never going to be overturned and nor should it be used to mask another United debacle.

As the enormity of the task he has taken on dawned upon him in the second half, the Liverpool fans taunted: 'Poch is the wheel.'

Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Man United head coach ended in a 4-0 defeat at Liverpool

The manner of the display was a microcosm of why United are mired in the relegation zone

Pochettino made two changes to the line-up from Michael Carrick's last game in charge against Aston Villa, and the biggest of them backfired spectacularly.

Giving Matthijs de Ligt his Premier League start for more than a year against Liverpool at Anfield felt like a gamble as he replaced Harry Maguire in central defence.

'When I saw Matthijs de Ligt's name on the team-sheet I was absolutely stunned,' admitted former United defender Gary Neville on Sky Sports, citing De Ligt's performance on his only start since last November in the Champions League defeat by Como in October.

However, the Dutchman was at fault for misreading the situation that led to Yoro being sent off in the eighth minute for the foul on Alexander Isak that saw Dominik Szoboszlai fire Liverpool ahead from a free-kick, and was the nearest United defender to Florian Wirtz when he hooked in the second shortly afterwards.

De Ligt got away with falling flat on his face and allowing Isak a free run on goal just after the hour mark, but couldn't stop Bradley Barcola's cross going through his legs when Rio Ngumoha scored the third shortly afterwards.

The nightmare was complete when his ill-judged pass to Joshua Zirkzee let in Liverpool for Victor Munoz to make it 4-0.

Pochettino's other change was to leave out Amad Diallo - who has claimed a couple of memorable goals against Liverpool but hasn't scored for United in nearly a year - and play Patrick Dorgu on the left.

Dorgu returned from injury to head a dramatic late equaliser in Carrick's final game in charge, but he was deemed to be unfit for duty by Denmark who sent him home during the international break.

He started on the left side of attack but switched to left-back when Yoro was sent off and Pochettino reshuffled what is statistically the worst defence in Europe as he tried to avoid a bloodbath.

Matthijs de Ligt (right) endured a nightmare game at centre-back as United were thumped

Pochettino's response to a horror start was to send on Maguire for Bryan Mbeumo, his best attacker, to provide extra protection for De Ligt.

Having started the game in United's familiar 4-2-3-1 formation, he switched to 5-3-1. Moving to a back-five when your team only has 10 men felt like damage limitation.

It needed some excellent saves from Senne Lammens - not to mention a crucial block by Maguire to send Isak's effort over the bar before half-time - to spare United from an embarrassing defeat on a par with the seven and five goal humiliations at the hands of Liverpool in recent years.

Even so, after seeing his team record a pitiful xG of 0.14 in a first half that saw United have one shot on target and four touches in the Liverpool box, he knew they had to pose more of an attacking threat if only to relieve the pressure on their defence.

Zirkzee replaced the anonymous Matheus Cunha at half-time in the hope that he could hold the ball up better, but the xG rose only marginally to 0.63 by the end compared to Liverpool's 4.38.

Pochettino sent on Mason Mount and Noussair Mazraoui for Youri Tielemans and Dorgu in the 65th minute, and they had only been on the pitch for a matter of seconds when Ngumoha got Liverpool's third.

Senne Lammens produced multiple save to prevent the scoreline from further embarrasment

There are so many problems piled up for Pochettino, it will be difficult to know where to start when he returns to his desk at Carrington on Monday ahead of this week's Champions League tie against Sporting Lisbon in Portugal.

This is a team chronically short of form and confidence that has forgotten how to win. There are only so many changes he can make with the squad available until the January transfer window, so the Argentine is stuck with what he's got until then.

But United have simply got to stop giving up early goals. It was a problem that plagued Carrick against Atletico Madrid, Como, Roma and Villa, and any hope that Pochettino could stop the rot disappeared inside eight minutes here.

Yoro's red card was also United's fourth in the last eight games (and his second), which is another bad habit they will have to kick if Pochettino is going to turn this season from hell around.

#1210. Genoa defender Ostigard spends night in hospital with high fever

Genoa defender Leo Ostigard spent Monday night in hospital after suffering a sudden high fever, although tests have since ruled out anything serious.

According to ANSA, the Norway international was taken to Genoa’s San Martino Hospital in the early hours, after the fever came with a severe headache.

He was examined by infectious disease specialist Professor Matteo Bassetti and his team. The routine diagnostic tests came back reassuring and ruled out any significant medical problems. Ostigard will nonetheless remain under observation at the hospital for the rest of today.

The scare came just a day after one of his best performances of the season. Ostigard was among Genoa’s standout players as Daniele De Rossi’s side won 2-0 at Sassuolo on Sunday, with Milutin Osmajić scoring both goals and the defence keeping a clean sheet.

That result made it three wins in four league games for the Grifone, who are 10th on 16 points.

Genoa will hope to have their defender back for a demanding week. They visit Inter at San Siro on Saturday at 20:45 CET [19:45 GMT], before facing the Nerazzurri again in the Coppa Italia next Tuesday.

#1209. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#1208. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1207. ‘King Kev’ – Man City fans pay tribute to De Bruyne ahead of Napoli clash

Manchester City supporters gave Kevin De Bruyne an emotional welcome on his return to the Etihad Stadium with Napoli in the Champions League tonight.

As noted by the Corriere dello Sport, the home fans greeted the Belgian with his famous “Oh Kevin De Bruyne” chant, which rang around the stadium for a decade.

A small banner with his picture and the words “King Kev” was also on display.

Cards showing De Bruyne in a City shirt were handed out in the stands, carrying the message: “Our King. If we know you’re happy every day, that’s enough for us.” Another read: “Once a Blue, always a Blue.”

You can follow all the action from the match, as it happens, on our Live Blog.

The tribute comes as no surprise given what De Bruyne achieved in Manchester. He arrived from Wolfsburg in 2015, amid some doubts after an unsuccessful spell at Chelsea, and became the creative heart of Pep Guardiola’s side.

In 10 years at the club, he won six Premier League titles, two FA Cups, five League Cups and the Champions League. He scored 108 goals and provided 177 assists in 421 appearances.

City had already given him a farewell fit for a king in May 2025, with a giant tifo, a mural in the city and a road at the club’s training ground named after him.

#1206. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#1205. ON THE ROAD: Clyde welcome their noisy new sponsors for some HEAVY METAL FOOTBALL

Published: 13:40 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 11:19 EST, 24 November 2026

Big in Japan. It is a term that modern beat combos use for overseas success. It applies equally to Clyde FC, purveyors of association football for 150 years, who now have a Japanese owner. Or two or three.

‘We have 1,100 owners in 59 countries,’ a club official tells me as the supporters’ lounge in New Douglas Park fills with fans of both football and Bleed From Within, a heavy metal group.

This fusion has been created by the band’s sponsorship of Clyde’s third strip. It is the latest example of the club’s innovative thinking.

‘Clyde Worldwide is a key part, we want to spread the word of the club all over,’ says chief executive David Alexander of the ownership scheme. ‘We would like these fans to become actively involved. It costs 60 quid a year but we don’t just want them to sit on the sidelines. We could use their skills and expertise.’

Indeed, one American owner has applied to join the board and will soon be up for election.

The owners come from the USA, Indonesia, Nigeria, Costa Rica and the Faroe Islands among many other different locations.

Clyde have partnered with Scottish metalcore band Bleed From Within

Band members Craig Gowans, Steven Jones and lead singer Scott Kennedy

‘We don’t have a community in the sense that we don’t have a permanent home of our own,’ says Alexander. ‘So this is a way to create excitement and a bit of a buzz. I am a believer that if you get the basics right at a club then everything falls into place.’

He adds: ‘We still have to find a home. That is the key point. We are still pursuing Stepford in Glasgow but we are awaiting the council on that. But we are stressing that we will be a positive for any venue in that we will bring people, bring investment, we will build things up. But we do the best we can while we are here.’

It was an hour before kick-off. An hour earlier, a punter walked into the fan zone carrying the news that the Bleed From Within shirt had sold out.

‘We ordered 500 from the manufacturers thinking that would be enough. But in the first couple of hours of the sale online we knew we had to think about re-ordering more,’ says Alexander. ‘After 24 hours we had sold four times the amount of our home kit,’ he says. Other merchandise has sped across the world as a result of Clyde Worldwide. The global match stream was offered at a discount to celebrate Bleed From Within day. It was a bargain with seven goals in a smashing match.

Clyde, The Movie, may be the sequel to Clyde, the heavy metal musical. ‘I love football and I love history and was looking at the stories here outside of Celtic and Rangers,’ says Bryan Wendland, a filmmaker from New York who now lives in Glasgow.

‘This is a historic Glasgow team who have not played in Glasgow since the eighties. The club trying to find a way back into the city was an interesting story that would have a lot of branches to follow.’

Wendland, 35, who has made short films in his homeland, plans for the Clyde project to be a feature film or series. It is a long-term project and ideally it needs Clyde to find a home in Glasgow.

The exile from Glasgow has fascinated Wendland. ‘I have been surprised at how many people have deep roots in the fandom of this club,’ he says.

He believed that the decades away from Glasgow would have destroyed that lineage of support. However, the strand of family support is still strong. ‘That is both surprising and moving,’ says Wendland.

‘I love generational stories,’ he says. ‘I support teams in America because my father supported them.’

Unwittingly, he is sitting in the fan zone across from one of the best examples of this syndrome.

Stephen Muckalt, a retired driver, is a third generation Bully Wee fan. ‘I have only missed seven games in 45 years,’ he says. ‘I first went to Shawfield in 1971 when I was seven. The family is from Rutherglen so I followed my grandfather and father to Shawfield.

‘The demise of Oatlands and Dalmarnock in terms of population has historically hit the club hard but there is still a good core who come from Rutherglen. I watch them every week.’

Clyde are flying high in League Two and sport their new kit

‘Stupidity,’ he says with a laugh. ‘No, it’s a love of the club. I have been kitman, in charge of the ball boys, I ran a school of football, so I have done my stint.’

He points out that the crucial issue is finding a home for the club. ‘We are nomads and we need somewhere to settle,’ he says. ‘If this was in Rutherglen, it would be ideal.’

A father and daughter have made the trip from Paisley, but not primarily to watch the football. Ian Donald and Jane Donald are fans of Bleed From Within.

‘I teach her good music,’ says Ian. ‘We have seen them a few times. She likes to stand at the front of the stage and I am a bit back. We have brought along a Saltire for the group to autograph. We love their style of music but we also love the fact that they are Scottish.’

He adds: ‘This is the first time I have been at New Douglas Park. I support Rangers and my daughter supports Celtic.’

Music has the power to cross all divides.

There is a mystery. ‘I just don’t know,’ says Steven Jones, when asked how the name of Bleed From Within came about. It was there when he joined the band 10 years ago.

The band meet supporters before Clyde take on Stirling Albion

And sign autographs for Clyde fans that believe a return to League One is within reach

He is, though, sure of the band’s love of football.

‘We all come from south Lanarkshire and love the game,’ he says. ‘We had a band strip made for Scotland in the World Cup and that went so well we were open to this. This sponsorship supports Scottish football so we are all for it.’

The link with Clyde is geographical. ‘We rehearsed out of a building in Dalmarnock for 10 or 11 years so we kind of contracted an affection for the club there,’ he says.

Three of the band walk into the fan zone to be greeted by applause and requests for autographs.

‘This is a bit of a strange gig for us,’ says Jones. ‘We are not here to play music so that makes it unusual for us but the afternoon has been great.’

The weirdest gig for the band in his eyes was one in eastern Czechoslovakia, as it then was. ‘We had to drive hours to this place and there were only 25 people there. The hall was like the scene of a vampire movie but it went well.’

The highlight was supporting Slipknot on their 2023 tour of the UK. ‘We used to say when things were not going great in the early days that we would look back on it all and laugh when we were supporting Slipknot. And then it happened.’

The world has a way of producing such surprises. Like Clyde shirts selling out and owners throughout the world watching a Scottish League Two match in a variety of international time zones.

#1204. US science academy urges journals to fix errors more quickly

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J. Richards/AFP via Getty

Science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds. Standards for fixing errors are also inconsistently applied across research journals, it says.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science

There are no data on how long retraction or correction currently takes, as journals do not generally disclose when they were alerted to a problem in a paper; the NASEM report says they should. On average, according to the Retraction Watch database, retractions occur around 2.4 years after a paper is published. The report recommends that editorial review processes be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months — at least when editors are looking at concerns over a single paper.

“The big picture is, the process is too slow,” says Randy Schekman, a cell biologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who chaired the 14-person committee that produced the NASEM report. A prompter and more transparent process would strengthen the reliability of the scientific record, he says.

The report was due to be published online on 19 November, but publication was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained some references with fabricated first names for authors, a possible sign that large language models had been used to write or edit the material and had been insufficiently checked.

“It's unfortunate that there were these flawed references in a report about fixing the literature,” says Jennifer Byrne, a cancer researcher and research integrity sleuth at the University of Sydney who first flagged the concern to Science when reviewing the report, which was shared ahead of publication with media outlets.

The report had two main aims: to speed up the process of retraction or correction and to lower the “tremendous emotional barriers” for authors to correct honest mistakes in the record, Schekman says. “Part of the problem is that it’s too rare for a paper to be retracted,” he adds.

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

The report also suggests that journals shouldn’t just wait for complaints to reach them, but instead “take proactive steps” to identify errors and integrity issues. That might include journal-wide audits, or regularly monitoring social media and online platforms where post-publication issues are raised, it says.

Existing guidelines for publishers, such as those from the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in London, only urge a “timely” response to concerns without setting out expected schedules, and don’t suggest journals scan online platforms for complaints.

“A major theme running through the report is that we have to distinguish between retraction or correction, and research misconduct,” notes Dorothy Bishop, a research-integrity sleuth in Oxford, UK, who was on the NASEM committee. Authors shouldn’t associate retracting a paper with the stigma of misconduct, she says. And although journal editors sometimes wait for a university to investigate whether there is research misconduct before correcting a paper, they shouldn’t, she adds.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Calls for changing these attitudes aren’t new: journals have long emphasized that retractions can cover honest mistakes. When it comes to journal processes, Holden Thorpe, the editor in chief of Science, urged that issuing corrections or retractions and making a determination of misconduct be separated in an editorial in 2022, and COPE guidelines already emphasize the point. But “there are still plenty of people who see a correction or retraction as an allegation of fraud,” says Thorpe, who was also on the NASEM committee. “Hopefully, this report will accelerate the recognition of the distinction,” he says.

#1203. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

Superb finish by Victor Munoz to level the scores here. Brentford were caught upfield and they were in trouble from the moment Florian Wirtz was able to slide the ball in behind for the Spanish winger. It comes as Liverpool were just starting to make their numerical advantage count.

Fulham are still dominating the ball and have been by far the better side. Their possession share remains in the high seventies. They’ve completed 476 passes to Hull’s 94.

The referee is sent to the pitchside monitor after a lengthy delay and Yarmoliuk is off!

We’ve had the second VAR review in just a few minutes here, and this one has resulted in a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk for a “headbutting action”. I have to say, this feels harsh. Brentford take the lead, and it’s a lead they probably just about deserve on the run of play. It’s an absolutely superb header by Keane Lewis-Potter, up from left-back, as he thumps Igor Thiago’s cross into the top corner of Liverpool’s net. Textbook technique.

Just after Wirtz was denied a penalty of his own, Mac Allister looks to have won a spot-kick for real off a challenge from Outtara. The referee gives it, but is then sent to the monitor and the decision is reversed. Correct decision. Outtara clearly got a piece of the ball first.

Brentford are getting the ball forward quickly, and Kelleher is the one to initiate the latest move. He finds Thiago on the halfway line, who gets the ball back off Outtara, but the Brazilian’s effort is well blocked by Van Dijk.

Before that Phil Foden sent a message to Thomas Tuchel with the opening goal. Foden, playing in central midfield, was left out of the last England squad and has seen Alex Scott climb above him in the pecking order. But Scott is injured for next month’s international which may give Foden a chance.

A defensive mix-up allowed the Frenchman a clear run at goal, one-on-one with Brentford’s Caoimhin Kelleher, but his finish was woeful. Huge boos and whistles for the Premier League anthem at the Etihad Stadium, with the final part of it drowned out by chants of “City, City, City.” Fans have made their feelings clear after the guilty verdict from the competition’s independent commission, with the club appealing the decision.

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1202. Krösche ‘operational’ with Milan announcement seemingly imminent

Markus Krösche is already in Milan and hard at work, even though his appointment as the Rossoneri’s new Head of Football is yet to be made official.

According to transfer expert Matteo Moretto, speaking on Fabrizio Romano’s YouTube channel, the German executive has already got down to business ahead of the January window.

“Markus Krösche is already in Milan, already very operational, despite it not being official yet, but the announcement is expected shortly,” Moretto said, via MilanNews24.

Krösche has long been Gerry Cardinale’s first choice.

On 18 October, he was released from his duties at Eintracht Frankfurt with immediate effect at his own request.

Milan and Eintracht have now reportedly reached an agreement over compensation, exchanging documents yesterday, with the Rossoneri paying around €4m.

Krösche’s first job will be Adrien Rabiot’s contract renewal.

“There’s a lot of work going on over Rabiot’s renewal. Cardinale’s intention is to close it by the end of the year, because Rabiot is an indispensable player for Ruben Amorim,” Moretto explained.

“Then we’ll see how the market develops. Milan want to strengthen up front, and Endrick is one name.”

Rabiot is under contract until June 2028, and Milan are reportedly working towards a new deal until 2030. Cardinale said on Sunday that any January signing will only come if it’s “a move that counts”.

#1201. LA communities kick out Big Oil

After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

#1198. Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

#1197. Self-serving Scottish clubs were always going to ensure Craig Mulholland's youth football revolution was doomed to failure

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:01 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 24 November 2026

Given how quickly things have unravelled under Sebastien Pocognoli, serious questions are now being asked of those in power at the Scottish Football Association.

Ian Maxwell and Craig Mulholland, the chief executive and chief football officer who led the recruitment process, certainly talked a good game when Pocognoli was appointed.

However, when Mulholland took up his position in the summer, his remit was much broader than merely the appointment of a new head coach for the national team. He was tasked with trying to initiate a much-needed revamp of youth development throughout Scottish football.

Only a few months into the job, those plans have already hit the buffers due to resistance from clubs, despite the obvious need for more young Scottish players to play more first-team football.

The SFA had proposed including two Under-21 players starting in cup competitions and the same age group playing a minimum of 6 per cent of all available minutes across a season in league competition.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland has met resistance in his bid to shake up the game

When it immediately became clear that several clubs in Scotland weren’t keen on that, a new watered-down version was then put back on the table.

Now there have been reports that those plans might be booted even further into the long grass and possibly won’t even be voted on at all this season.

As is always the case, the self-serving interest from clubs in Scotland will always trump the need for national reform.

But that is only part of the story. What is also of serious concern is the lack of quality coaching afforded to players in academies across the country.

If that was to be addressed, clubs would perhaps feel more obliged to play more younger players if they were ready for first-team football.

It is a multi-faceted problem – and one which Mulholland is no closer to solving. Clubs are selfish and will serve their own needs, with no obligation to buy into any new proposals.

The SFA could stand firm and try to force some of these plans through as non-negotiable. A tough stance, albeit one that risks becoming messy.

But nobody should be naïve enough to believe that self-interest from the clubs is the root of all problems here. It is much, much deeper than that.
