#1106. NWSL, U.S. Soccer continue focus on women's soccer growth with player and executive development programs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – The NWSL has always been a measuring stick for the growth of women's soccer in the U.S., which in recent years has been headlined by skyrocketing expansion fees and increased fan engagement. There's a buzzword that continues to pop up around the league, one that is rarely associated with the key performance indicators – pipeline. After she read out another list of attendance figures and viewership numbers before the 2026 season wraps up with Saturday's NWSL Championship (8 p.m. ET, CBS, Paramount+), commissioner Jessica Berman made a hard pivot in her state of the league remarks on Thursday to say the league is officially in the business of prioritizing said pipeline.

In the first of four announcements she teased was in service of that. The NWSL announced two initiatives on Thursday: the creation of a player development rule (PDR) and a sporting executive leadership program, designed specifically to focus on the foundation of the league's structure. The plans are a marriage of the league's business model and sporting objectives, a tacit understanding that the two go hand-in-hand, especially for a league that is admittedly driven by star power. These new plans, though, are hardly the only initiatives that will influence the pipeline.

The NWSL's new initiatives reflect a shifting focus across the American soccer landscape, one that seems driven by the heightened interest in the sport courtesy of this year's World Cup in North America. The league's financial stability enabled this shift but beyond that, there are overlapping commitments across the industry to finally fix one of American soccer's most evident problems – the pipeline. The sport's success in this country has often come in spite of a fractured youth soccer system, one that U.S. Soccer hopes to unite in the coming years.

The parties, be it in conjunction or individually, are also dead set on ensuring the women's game is held in equal regard to the men's every step of the way.

The PDR joins a list of NWSL rules in recent years that have incentivized clubs to recruit young players more easily such as the U-18 Entry Mechanism and organizing its first-ever combine last year. The new rule requires participating clubs to develop a curriculum that supports player development and is tied directly to salary cap relief.

"What can we do at the league to motivate and incentivize clubs to develop players?" Sarah Gregorius, the NWSL's vice president of sporting, told CBS Sports. "What do we have in our toolkit? And one of the things we obviously have in our toolkit is a salary cap and we can use that as a motivation and as an incentive to encourage the types of behavior around player development that we want to see, and hopefully, it's really our first structural foray into player development. Again, it's deliberately an incentive. It's not a mandate. It's up to the clubs. If they want to participate, if they want to access the reward, they know what they have to do in order to do that."

There is a perceived industry standard about developing young players, even if it is as far from an exact science as it gets. Academy systems tied to clubs are how players often come up the ranks – that is true across the men's game including in MLS and increasingly so for women's players in Europe. The NWSL does not have a streamlined system that mirrors the academy set-up and interestingly enough, is not actually trying to go in that direction.

"This is a pretty unique country," Gregorius said. "It doesn't actually work to pick something up from overseas and plop it down over here and I'm actually not convinced in the two years that I've spent here and everything that I've learned that this vertical academy system across the clubs makes the most sense. There's already a ton of incredible player development happening. There's just a bit of a lack of cohesion and a lack of connection to the professional game … The Spanish model won't work here, the German model wouldn't work here, the Japanese model wouldn't work here. Got a ton of respect for what they're doing in their countries but the reason that it works is it's for those countries. We have to do something that works for this one, which has characteristics that no other country in the world has. F---, this place is big. It's dynamic. There's a lot going on."

Gregorius believes a league-issued mandate might further fracture an already splintered landscape.

"If I think about it from a local level, some of our clubs are in markets that have thriving youth ecosystems, right?" Gregorius started. "So if all of a sudden there was a mandate from the league that every single club – which is what they do in England – has to come in and have a professional game academy, they're going to all of a sudden have to start pulling players out of those environments, which is disruptive for the kids. It's disruptive for the families. Some of those kids and families are also fans of the team. It's the icing on the cake in those particular markets so all of a sudden, you create tension. You create tension for the parents. You create tension for the kids. You create tension within the fan groups. They're like, 'Well, no, actually. You've stripped out my youth club in order to service a mandate from the league, not paying attention to the fact that all of your talented players have come through the system.' That's not what we want. That's bad for player development and it's bad for fan engagement, to be honest."

The NWSL is distinguishing itself from MLS, a league to which it has no formal ties but one that committed to the traditional academy system over a decade ago and can count it amongst its greatest successes. There's no stigma associated with the diverging path, though – U.S. Soccer has committed to viewing the women's game specifically through a female lens in recent years, an initiative championed by U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes but embraced by many, either through her influence or separate from it.

"The intense focus on the pathway is very intentional," U.S. Soccer COO Dan Helfrich told CBS Sports. "The intense focus as we build the next version of the women and girls pathway, that it's done through a female lens, is very intentional and look, there is going to be, we believe, historic investment and interest in women's soccer and it's it's going to crescendo into the 2031 World Cup and making sure we take advantage of this moment to corral and direct the investment and interest in a sustainable way. I don't think there's anything that could have a greater legacy for women's soccer in our country than that."

The distinction between the men's and women's games, even at the youth levels, is easy for Helfrich to make because they have always existed.

"The first thing is the environments for players to develop in," he said. "it's really important that they're tailored to women and girl  and that includes environments for youth clubs and colleges and professional clubs and so some of the work, for example, of the Kang Women's Institute becomes really important to do the research to develop the insights and then for us to promulgate them into all these areas, that's different and if you look at the as-is state of the pathway, the league structures for girls are different than the league structures for boys. The role of college soccer for girls is different than the role of college soccer for boys and so practically, if you're trying to optimize a future, you apply a different lens."

There's more shared consensus when it comes to developing leaders that will foster players' growth, which is where the sporting executive leadership program kicks in. The program is built around specialized education for sporting director types, the first yearlong edition of the initiative already in session. A cohort of six – Haley Carter of the Washington Spirit, Caitlin Carducci of the Orlando Pride, Angela Mangano of the Houston Dash, Jeff Agoos of the Portland Thorns, Kelly Cousins of the Utah Royals and Dome Guasch of the Boston Legacy – already took part in their first session of a project supported both by U.S. Soccer and FIFA.

"The 16, now 18, individuals who hold the highest sporting position at the clubs have an outsized impact on the on-field identity and on-field product of their club so therefore, all of those people have an an impact on the on-field product of the league," Gregorius noted. "It's also, curiously enough, one of the few roles within the sporting department that doesn't have a license. You don't need to have completed a particular license. There's no education requirements or anything like that so when we also did an audit of the 16 clubs and who was holding those positions, some have former players, some have lawyers, some have people with an operations background, some have people with a coaching background. It was very varied so we're like, okay, if we know that this group has a ton of impact, if we know that they don't go through any structured learning. Is there a way that we can wrap our arms around them and support them?"

The uniqueness of this program is that it is tied specifically to the NWSL, which operates independently of a men's league unlike some of its European counterparts or even the WNBA.

"It's the first of its kind because every other f---ing part of the world just cares about men's football so we're really, really proud of not only the commitment and the discipline around trying to get it off the ground," Gregorius said.

It is in parallel with other initiatives the league and U.S. Soccer have worked on in recent years. The NWSL combine, for example, was also an effort to bolster female coaches while U.S. Soccer frequently uses its new national training center to conduct coaching courses with the youth game in mind.

"What I would say is to grow the game the way it needs to be grown, we can't underestimate or overlook the non-player part of development," Helfrich said, "and the non-player part of development is coaches. The non-player part of development is scouts. Non-player part of development is referees and the non-player part of development is front office, technical leaders and so, building a partnership with the NWSL on all of those important non-player development activities is a big priority."

The NWSL's partnership with U.S. Soccer on this program also speaks to a unique truth about American soccer. The women's game is held in incredibly high regard in the U.S. because of the historic success of the USWNT, who have four World Cup titles and five Olympic gold medals in their 40-year history. The USWNT's reputation of being serial winners is intrinsically tied to the health of the federation, the NWSL and in some ways, American soccer as a whole.

"Honest to God, I've loved waking up every day and only thinking about the women's game," Gregorius, a former New Zealand international, said. "It's brilliant and it's very unique over here that we are able to do that and what I love about working with U.S. Soccer, as well, to be honest, is they're the same. They're almost more interested in the women's game sometimes than they are anything else … It's an organization that is already on the train, you know what I mean? The NWSL and our clubs, it's not even a question of being in the shadow of the men's game or any of that other bulls--- that you kind of encounter in other places. The focus is unwavering and that's brilliant."

#1105. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

Is artificial intelligence putting entry-level jobs in science at risk? As the technology increasingly takes on coding and basic data analysis, alongside other purely cognitive tasks, what will happen to graduate student and postdoctoral roles? And what does the future hold for programmers and technicians? These roles have conventionally been stepping stones to other scientific positions.

#1103. NWSL Championship 2026 picks: Will the Washington Spirit or the Kansas City Current reach the top?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the third straight time, the Washington Spirit are playing for the NWSL Championship. The No. 3 Spirit host the No. 4 Kansas City Current at Audi Field on Saturday for the biggest prize in domestic women's soccer. Kickoff is at 8 p.m. ET, and you can see it all on CBS and Paramount+.

The Washington Spirit won it all in 2021 but came up just short in each of the last two finals. This may be the day that Trinity Rodman gets her second crown.

The Kansas City Current bring plenty to the final and may just be the favorites. They're back in the big game for the first time since 2022 after ending NJ/NY Gotham FC's title defense in the semis. Croix Bethune, who used to play for the Spirit, curled in a free-kick stunner, and Haley Hopkins won it in the 89th minute.

So who lifts the trophy? Our experts make their picks below.

Star-studded attack: This year's finalists did not have the most straightforward journeys to the NWSL Championship, but the good news for each of them is that there will be few excuses when they finally take to the pitch on Saturday. Trinity Rodman is about to cap off a career-best campaign after an injury-riddled 2025 season and will be joined by the impactful Sofia Cantore and midseason arrival Clara Luvanga, putting the Washington Spirit in as good a position as any to come out with a win that has eluded them over the last two seasons. The Current, though, are in the same boat --  they have struggled without their all-star trio, but each of Croix Bethune, Temwa Chawinga and Michelle Cooper will be available on Saturday and equally capable of turning the game in their favor.

Midfield battles: There's going to be a real display of veteran prowess and eager energy. Both teams have experienced players and rising stars, and it'll be a combo of chess and tug of war during the NWSL Championship. Washington Spirit's Andi Sullivan anchors most things in the middle, with Leicy Santos linking play and Melissa Bethi's recent rise in form. Even with all the changes from injuries to departures and returns from maternity leave, the Spirit are gelling at a good time in a crucial part of the pitch. They'll battle against Kansas City's Lo'eau LaBonta and Vanessa DiBernardo, two of the best in the league with longevity and finesse. Ball knowers understand that they're two players who can control a game, close and create lanes, or serve up goals and assists. Add attacking mid Croix Bethune into the mix, and Kansas City have plenty of ways to win the middle of the park.  -- Sandra Herrera

Balance: At their best, the Washington Spirit are a side who can win a game in multiple ways, and while there's plenty of star power on both sides, balance is where they win out. It's a fascinating match for both sides and one where the margins will be thin but being able to have a strong attack led by Trinity Rodman along with a buildup that Andi Sullivan keeps control of. If the Spirit can control the pace, it will be a long day for Kansas City but Croix Bethune will have ideas of her own as well.  -- Chuck Booth

Washington Spirit: The Spirit have tossed around the phrase that the third time's the charm after two empty-handed trips to the NWSL Championship and this year, it's hard not to buy the argument. Rodman is happy and healthy but she is just one part of a team that has been smartly assembled over the years and seems as cohesive as ever. -- Pardeep Cattry

Washington Spirit: Truthfully, the pressure is on the Washington Spirit headed into this one, and that typically doesn't play out the best for teams who are the higher seed or considered favorites on paper. Kansas City will be a more than worthy opponent, but the Spirit's third time in the final comes with a long home build-up through and back to Audi Field, and any mental component needed will come with a boost from the crowd environment. -- Sandra Herrera

Washington Spirit: Sure, this is a "neutral" venue, but being a home team in a final match will carry the Spirit at Rowdy Audi. Considering that this is the third consecutive final, fans snatched up tickets as soon as they could, assuming that the home side would be here. While all the pressure is on the Spirit and rightfully so, the team has also embraced that, and once the first goal goes in the net, this is going to turn into a party.  -- Chuck Booth

Trinity Rodman: Is this an obvious choice? Yes, yes it is, but to be fair, Rodman has earned the right to be the easy pick. She has always been key to the Spirit's success but hit a new level this season, to the point that she had a very valid MVP case even if her ex-teammate Ashley Sanchez took it home instead after a record-breaking season with the North Carolina Courage. Rodman's ability to create and score chances means she's very likely to have a say on Saturday, one that could very well end the Spirit's five-year wait for another championship. -- Pardeep Cattry

Clara Luvanga: The last few NWSL Championship MVPs have gone to the lone goal scorer. Barbra Banda won it in 2024 for her game-winning goal, and Rose Lavelle earned it for her single title goal in 2025. If these two teams match up on the pitch as evenly as they do on paper, then it could come down to a single moment again, and Luvanga has shown she's better positioned for it with her current form. Her four goals and three assists through seven games make her an efficient threat on goal, and could finally be the difference maker for the group in their third final. -- Sandra Herrera

Trinity Rodman: To win finals, you need your best players to be at their best. All eyes have been on Trinity Rodman this season after she became the highest-paid player in NWSL history, and she has delivered. Considering that the next development in her career is to become a player for the biggest moments, and capping off the final by scoring will be just the way to do it. -- Chuck Booth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Bayern Munich's depth was already pushed to the limit, but Friday's 1-1 draw with Koln may have broken Vincent Kompany's side. Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane lasted only 20 minutes before exiting with what the club is calling a "syndesmosis ligament tear in his left ankle," which required surgery overnight and will keep him sidelined "for months," according to sporting director Max Eberl.

"Harry Kane underwent successful surgery overnight after tearing his left ankle ligament in yesterday's home match against 1. FC Köln. The 33-year-old will now begin his rehab," Bayern said in a statement.

Counting down the days already ❤️‍🩹 pic.twitter.com/rpNWUxc4vW

Losing Kane alone is a significant blow to the Bavarians after they failed to replace Nicolas Jackson when his loan ended, but the injuries didn't stop there. Michael Olise was also withdrawn at halftime and left the stadium on crutches.

This led to a match in which Bayern put only one shot on target against a side just above the relegation zone, showing this is a problem of their own creation in the transfer market. Coming into the season without a viable backup for an aging Kane would eventually hurt Bayern, and Kompany now needs to oversee a worst-case scenario. Luis Diaz and Ismael Saibari were already out with injuries, and when Kane went down, Thomas Bischof had to come in for him instead of a like-for-like striker. Even with Jamal Musiala's neurological issues, the players they do have aren't able to perform at their best.

Already in an actual title race in the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund, these are the kinds of setbacks that can lead to a new German champion for the first time since Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24, and even they had to go undefeated to accomplish that feat, while this season could be Bayern's own undoing. They've been one of the top sides in the world when healthy, but as it is, this side will struggle in Champions League play, where they'll travel to face Lille. Precariously in 13th place in the Champions League league phase, Bayern won't fall out of the top 24 without Kane, but it could get close to something that they should be concerned about. Even missing out on the top eight and needing to play additional games is something that Bayern won't want to deal with, considering this injury crisis.

Being a backup to Kane is a thankless task, as it's hard to get game time and you're also compared to one of the best players in the world, but it's still a multifaceted failure for Bayern to not have one. Real Madrid were able to recruit post-prime players to back up Karim Benzema, and now Kylian Mbappe has a backup from the academy. There's no reason that a club of Bayern's stature shouldn't be able to do the same, but here we are in the same position they constantly find themselves in.

Depth issues have held Bayern back from claiming a Champions League title in recent years. Kane winning the Ballon d'Or solidified that the starting XI is more than good enough to lift Europe's most coveted club trophy, and the difference between this side and the 2020 one that won the Champions League is their lack of depth.

It's a strange situation with Musiala that isn't being handled well, with board members open to selling him, and it doesn't help the club's overall trajectory. Bayern will need to shake things up in January, but these issues began long before now, and to return to the top of the global game, they need to change the way they do things.

#1101. 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner said. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he said.

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color."

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

#1100. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and said “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

Could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

So it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

Aside from their stadium being called Highbury, Fleetwood Town’s red shirts with white sleeves also bear a striking resemblance to Arsenal’s home kit. The club in its current guise was founded in 1997, although previous iterations date back to 1908 under the name Fleetwood FC.

There is no evidence or anecdote suggesting Arsenal were the inspiration, so it appears the kit clash is a coincidence. Arsenal will be wearing their navy away strip.

The club’s most famous son is surely Jamie Vardy, who scored 31 goals in 36 appearances for Fleetwood in the 2011-12 season before Leicester City made their move.

An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”Full team news on the way shortly.

#1099. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

#1098. Leeds expose Chelsea's unresolved defensive problems as Xabi Alonso's crew yet to find footing

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- This was supposed to be the year, the time when Chelsea grew up and a proper manager started extracting consistent performances from a squad whose much-vaunted talent is too rarely expressed in results form. In this most in-flux of Premier League seasons, Xabi Alonso still might leave her with something. It is not going to take particular excellence for a club like this to achieve the bare minimum of Champions League qualification. Adequacy might do it.

Once more, however, that is threatening to be a standard beyond Chelsea. This 4-1 defeat at home to old rivals Leeds has them squeezed into the Premier League's middle ground, those above them very visible proof of how much more can be done with less. There is nothing false about that position. Since the last weeks of summer, Alonso's team have given up so much at the back that their likeliest route to success seemed to be supernova seasons from all three of Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro. Nothing else would paper over the cracks in the defense.

And Alonso has tried a lot. Right backs in midfield, center backs as nominal left wing backs that are actually auxiliary central midfielders, switching the right wing back to center forward: in isolation, you could make a case for so many of these adjustments. When the performances are so inconsistent, why not change the XI every game? Alonso's success at Bayer Leverkusen, coupled with the inquisitive footballing mind that made the player so beloved of elite coaches, have earned him the right to experiment.

Every change, however, begs the question of what the foundations underlying all this are. Those ought to have shone through this afternoon. Alonso's was as straightforward an XI as he has named. Estevao, Palmer and Rogers off an orthodox center forward, Moises Caicedo running the double pivot and an orthodox back four in front of Emiliano Martinez. This looked like a team intent on playing its way.

Instead, they had Leeds' game foisted upon them. That might have been different if they had not lost Caicedo. He seemed to have a handle on the game before colliding with James Justin as both competed for a high ball. Those often seemed like the only sort up for grabs today; even when Chelsea played well, they were playing the sort of game Leeds wanted. This wasn't quite the rapid attacking up the gut with which Xabi Alonso charmed the Premier League early in this season. It was bypass the press-ball, get it straight up to the final third and see what comes of it.

It can work. Justin, exemplary as a man-marker without the ball and roving agent of chaos in the Chelsea half, cleared a goal kick straight into the back of Morgan Rogers. He moved swiftly up the Leeds gut, his pass to Emmanuel Emegha delivered at just the right moment for the Premier League debutant to slam in the opener. It was perhaps the only moment of clinical execution from the Blues.

They needed so many more. After all, this is a team that fails to meet the standards in so many aspects of defending. They press like a newly promoted team. They always seem to name one defender who can be picked on in the duels (starting left back Pep Charravia ranks 101st of 102 defenders for duel success over 300-plus Premier League minutes). Midfielders routinely abandon runners. When Caicedo left this game the feint thread holding the team together was cut.

No one had the composure to deal with the bouncing ball moments after Emegha's opener, Noah Okafor free to move into the box and shoot low through a crowd of legs. No one seemed truly live to the danger for Okafor's second, thundered into the roof of the net when Chelsea could not repel pressure down their right. Between that a contentious penalty, Jayden Bogle's long-range effort striking Rogers right in the grey area between sleeve and arm. If that hadn't been the moment when Chelsea caved, another would have come along.

"Leeds believed more than us," Alonso admitted. "We didn't show a good enough reaction." The quick one-two punch had been more than enough to send Chelsea heads to the floor.

A two-goal deficit ought not to be beyond their reach, but the final 32 minutes saw them outshot seven to six with fewer passes completed into the penalty area. Palmer's most notable action of this game was to row with Joao Pedro as he made his way down the tunnel. Nothing he could have done would have overcome the problems Chelsea made for themselves at the other end. It really wouldn't hurt, though if he did more than nothing.

These feel like problems unresolved by a manager who was supposed to be the savior. Eleven Premier League games is not a lot to turn the tide but it is enough to give us a sense of who this team are. The answer is a team whose early scoring streak covered for a below-average attack (1.25 non-penalty expected goals per game, 14th in the Premier League) and a below-average defense (1.44 non-penalty expected goals allowed per game, 15th in the Premier League). The game state-warping impact of scoring with your first shot can only mitigate so much.

Is it time for a conversation about Alonso and pressure? If so it has to be caveated by the unity and purpose he fostered at Bayer Leverkusen, qualities this dressing room sorely needs. He might not have corralled the superstars at Real Madrid but the press and possession system he forged could have achieved great things given time. Stitching together a version of this Chelsea, overloaded with number 10s and underpowered defensive players, that suits the more direct and chaotic Premier League was always going to be a coaching challenge.

And of course this is not the Roman Abramovich era. Swapping out coaches is not a silver bullet for perennial trophy contenders but instead the modus operandi of an ownership group that are the most serious problem at Stamford Bridge. Someone is going to have to be afforded time to corral this squad or indeed tear it down and start again. Doing that is going to be a club-wide effort, including fans. Few of them hung around to wave off a side who had allowed old rivals Leeds a first win at Stamford Bridge since 1999, the same side who had let Tottenham break the habit of a lifetime last month.

The vibes are bad. The performances might be worse. This brand new start is feeling all too familiar.

#1097. Chelsea's slump in form unpacked: The stars who badly need to step up from Emi Martinez to Cole Palmer, what defensive horror shows mean for Xabi Alonso's job security - and the players in line to leave in January

Published: 12:00 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 12:02 EST, 23 November 2026

Chelsea are lurching towards a crisis after yet another loss in which they were bullied, this time by Leeds United.

That 4-1 hiding saw Xabi Alonso heckled, and his players booed at both half-time and full-time, arguably deservedly so for such a disastrous showing.

It has led to tentative speculation around Alonso's future as Chelsea prepare to travel to Oliver Glasner's Nottingham Forest on Friday night, not to mention questions about where he is going wrong and how he might arrest his team's slump in form.

Here, Daily Mail Sport tackles all the burning issues at Stamford Bridge...

Chief among Chelsea’s problems is the fact they have conceded 20 Premier League goals this season. It is as many as they have scored at the other end. So, as much as we have enjoyed their freescoring forward line this season, so too must we criticise their disastrous defending.

We know Alonso can organise a defence. His Bayer Leverkusen side only conceded 24 goals when they won the Bundesliga as unbeaten champions in 2023-24. Chelsea are now on the verge of overtaking that total before we even hit December.

Liam Delap, their former striker now at Forest, will be desperate to add to that tally this Friday, too.

Xabi Alonso is coming under growing pressure, with his Chelsea side failing to back up their promising early-season form

Levi Colwill was all at sea against Leeds as Chelsea shipped another four goals, taking their tally to 20 in 11 games

This morning, I watched back all 20 of the goals that Chelsea have leaked this term. There have been so many individual mistakes.

Like on day one, in the 3-2 win at Fulham, when an out of position Robert Sanchez let in Josh King's shot. And when Levi Colwill missed a defensive header which should have been routine, which led to Gonzalo Garcia scoring.

Chelsea got rid of Sanchez after that game, but Emiliano Martinez has hardly helped shore up this defence, as was apparent in the 4-1 loss to Leeds, when Colwill and Co were again all over the shop.

Until they cut out the silly mistakes, it is hard to see Chelsea competing at the top end of the Premier League.

Every manager at every club is sackable. Nobody is immune. But that’s not to say Alonso is suddenly up for the chop at Chelsea. I haven’t heard anything which would suggest those inside the club think finding a fourth permanent manager in the year 2026 is the answer.

Let’s not forget the overwhelming optimism when news broke of Chelsea striking an agreement to hire Alonso. It was an hour or so after the club had lost the 2026 FA Cup final to Manchester City. Recently, I took a look at the comments section of the story I wrote that day. It was full of excitement from Chelsea fans, and anger from Liverpool supporters at missing out on him.

Anyway, I think it’s too soon for us to start talking about Alonso’s job. He is in a bad moment, obviously. A very bad moment. Losing at home to Tottenham Hotspur and Leeds is a complete no-no for any Blues boss.

The supporters are more likely to curse his name than chant it right now, and it is hard to identify the style Alonso wants, with few discernible patterns of play to Chelsea's football.

But let’s give the bloke a chance to get himself out of this jam as he heads into his 12th Premier League match.

Believe it or not, Chelsea don’t like changing managers mid-season if they can help it. Enzo Maresca resigned, exiting on January 1, 2026. Liam Rosenior was sacked, yes, but the club were effectively forced into that change as the players clearly gave up on him. Let’s see if Alonso can find some solutions.

Chelsea don’t like changing managers mid-season if they can help it and Alonso, remember, has only had 11 Premier League games in charge

We’ve tried to coax a little anger out of Alonso at press conferences, practically encouraging him to have a pop at his players for how they are performing, but he tends to resist the urge.

He’s clearly a nice guy. However, a Chelsea source does tell me he’s different behind the scenes. We may not see it on the outside, but internally, he is perfectly capable of being fiery with the players.

Which I hope is the case. Because sometimes, it can feel as if these Chelsea players need a good kick up the backside, rather than being coddled.

I wrote a piece after the 4-1 loss to Leeds about how superstars can be stroppy. It’s normal. They can be so good that when the game isn’t going their way, they show their sulky side.

Palmer did that both during and after Saturday’s defeat. It was pretty poor from him to not want to go around applauding the fans who had bothered to stick around at full-time, even if there had been boos. An apology has been attributed to Palmer on social media, but that’s just another case of fake quotes being circulated.

For me, Palmer has to look at himself as much as anybody. It’s been too long since we’ve seen him try to take a match by the scruff of the neck.

Cole Palmer put in another quiet display against Leeds - he needs to start taking matches by the scruff of the neck

WHAT HAPPENED WITH EMEGHA AFTER THE GAME?

Striker Emmanuel Emegha started for the first time and scored for the first time in Chelsea’s 4-1 loss to Leeds. Then he exited Stamford Bridge.

We have seen players leaving the stadium on foot before. Videos of Palmer being surrounded by supporters while being escorted to his ride home occasionally crop up on social media.

Emegha had possessions stolen from his car while he was in a restaurant after the match and the incident has been reported to police. He was not harmed.

From a footballing point of view, I'd like to see Emegha start away at Forest this Friday.

Not that I’m aware. He’s been linked with Paris Saint-Germain and I had an email from a PR person this morning trying to push a loan to AC Milan or Roma as a possibility.

Alonso has given the fans what they wanted in the last few league games. He started Estevao against Manchester United, brought him on at half-time at Sunderland and started him against Leeds.

Estevao, clearly an exciting talent, could do with taking these opportunities to show why he deserves more of them.

Estevao has been given a chance to shine by Alonso in recent weeks but has failed to grab his opportunities

I could see Malo Gusto leaving if there’s interest and Chelsea don’t keep demanding £75million, because it is hard to see who would spend that on him.

Gusto started in five of Alonso’s first six games in all competitions at the beginning of the campaign. Since then, he has been handed one start in eight, and that was in the Carabao Cup at Liverpool. Coming on as a substitute in the loss to Leeds, he tried and failed to play Brenden Aaronson offside and was then beaten by his man as the visitors made it 4-1.

I wouldn’t be surprised if a few other fringe players are linked with leaving in pursuit of game time ahead of January, such as Valentin Barco and Jamie Gittens, who is training again after his ankle injury.

As for incomings, I don’t need to tell you that Chelsea are interested in Alex Scott of Bournemouth. Arsenal are, too, but the word is the Blues are still the frontrunners as we approach January. Whether Scott is what this team needs is another conversation.

#1095. Vlatko Andonovski built it, Chris Armas finished it: KC Current's NWSL title was continuity through disruption

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – The Kansas City Current were built to experience a confetti shower, one they undoubtedly felt was not a moment too soon, even if it came a year later than expected. It is hard not to view their first-ever NWSL Championship, which came via a 2-1 win over the Washington Spirit on Saturday, as a continuation of last year's record-breaking Shield triumph and their consistency in recent years, boasting the most cumulative points out of any team in the last three seasons.

There was a trademark sense of inevitability that usually follows a team en route to victory, the Current dictating the game state and never looking back against the Spirit. This, though, was not a year of continuity for the Current.

There was a disruptive quality to their run to the championship, one that is inherently rooted in a decision to distance the architect of the project from the project itself. Chris Armas inherited a team built by Vlatko Andonovski, who first shifted to a sporting director role at the start of the season and then abruptly left in late summer in a move that inspired a wave of emotions from a squad that started to look like a title contender when Andonovski took charge in 2024. Armas began to work with a team that was already capable of winning a title and will be credited with seeing the vision through, all while putting his own spin on things. He also inherited a perfect set of circumstances, which ultimately got the Current over the finish line.

"I walked into a really good team," Armas said post-match. "There was a good culture built in. There was a lot of good pieces and that was one of the reasons that lured me to the club … My job as the head coach is just to try to assess the situation and through tough times help us be steady."

The Current won eight straight games to close out the season, a run in which they were at their best because they were at their strongest. Their championship-winning season can ultimately be split in two – the stretch of the season in which Temwa Chawinga, Michelle Cooper and Croix Bethune were all fit and available and the stretch of the season in which at least one was missing. It is understandable that the Current would rely on a trio like that one, especially as Bethune became a finishing touch of sorts when she arrived last winter. By design, the group was always going to bolster the Current's chances of going the distance.

"I'm relying on these amazing people and players to help keep things steady but we have talent all along," Armas continued. "We just had to get everyone back and healthy and then we knew we'd have a chance. The question would be, would we have enough time? And we had time, and they did the rest. We stayed steady. We have a great team and we peaked at the right time and now they're champions."

Their overreliance on them, though, did not matter when the business end of the season came. The Current's starry trio was ready; by default, so were the Current.

Armas' team is distinct from Andonovski's in several ways, as evidenced in the NWSL's most glittery moment of the season. Vanessa DiBernardo's olimpico opened the scoring in the second half was the most stylish way of the Current's increased emphasis on set pieces since Armas took over, a skill that was also incredibly useful in their semifinal win at Gotham FC.

VANESSA DIBERNARDO SCORES AN OLIMPICO IN THE NWSL CHAMPIONSHIP TO PUT KC CURRENT IN FRONT 🤯Stream all the @nwsl championship action on @cbs and @paramountplus. pic.twitter.com/dcZTivEoNt

"Lucas Rodriguez has been here from the literal day one," captain Lo'eau LaBonta said about set piece coach Lucas Rodriguez. "We have been talking about it for the last couple weeks, where we started and where we are now and, so, also that first year, it was his first time ever in women's soccer, so he's grown with the game as well, and he's learned the league and I think that's absolutely what helped him create these amazing set pieces to help us win the trophy."

The vestiges of Andonovski's team, though, are hard to miss. The journey that led them to Saturday's win was essentially a direct response to the NWSL Shield win that Andonovski oversaw a year ago, a race that was complete by the end of September, a whole month between their trophy lift and their 2025 quarterfinal defeat to Gotham.

"I think we needed to lose in those quarters almost to lift the trophy and win it all this year because it was just different," captain Lo'eau LaBonta said. "We won the Shield so early last year that we never really had that playoff mentality going into the playoffs because we had already been in it for so long so now that we've experienced everything on each side, I think we absolutely are going to use this to hopefully get help us going forward and make a legacy."

It is not a pattern that is unfamiliar in Armas' career, either. Saturday's championship is the first major title he collected as a coach since 2018, when he led MLS' New York Red Bulls to the Supporters' Shield. Though he was an assistant for several years in the build-up, he also inherited that team from Jesse Marsch, who left midseason for the start of an up-and-down coaching stint in Europe that began at Red Bull Salzburg. The success became hard to replicate; the Red Bulls finished sixth in 2019 and again in 2020, though Armas was out of a job before the season was up. He only managed a few months at Toronto FC, had his own adventures as an assistant coach in England with Ralf Rangnick's Manchester United and at the end of Marsch's ill-fated spell at Leeds United, and then led the Colorado Rapids to a seventh-place finish in 2024 and missed the playoffs in 2025.

Armas' Current exist in a fascinating in-between when it comes to the mold of championship-winning teams. They created a game state that rattled the Spirit from start to finish for the most part, notably doing so while staying true to the attacking identity Andonovski established. The key was creating a physical game state, one that they trialed at Gotham a week earlier and then turned the dial up on at the Spirit on Saturday. The plan worked – they limited the Spirit to just 0.77 expected goals from 18 shots, all while generating 2.32 from their 15.

"We are a physical team and there was a lot of whistles and a kind of disruptive play but at the end of the day, we do want to be disruptors so it doesn't matter," defender Kayla Sharples said. "We're going to keep that aggression. I think that's what we did and so we tried not to let it faze us. If anything, it kind of got us more hyped. We need to stay focused and have that mentality finishing off the game."

There's also the belief that championship-winning teams are often defined by their ability to survive in imperfect circumstances. Their record with and without their starry trio indicates one thing but with winners' medals around their necks, the Current's players believe they managed to strike the best of both worlds approach in order to win on Saturday. Time will tell if Armas can actually extend his streak, something he was unable to do at the Red Bulls. There were undoubtedly moments of adversity along the way, though, their playoff hopes far from a guarantee with five games left in the regular season and a consistency that at least resembles the 2025 Shield-winning campaign will be key in 2027.

"We kind of have the same style of play but I think Chris has done a great job being the fuel and the fire, making sure we're emphasizing certain details," Sharples said. "I think what we went through this year, where we learned a lot about resiliency and grit and we were down goals, we went and we came back to win and that's what you need in order to be successful at the end of the season, so I think that was, honestly, the big takeaway from the season, and it really helped us at the end of the day."
